questions.text: For prices p1 and p2 and income m, the consumer’s budget set consists of all bundles satisfying

options.b: p1x1 + p2x2 ≤ m.
options.d: p1x1 + p2x2 ≥ m.

questions.text: The budget line consists of bundles that

options.a: cost exactly the consumer’s income m.
options.b: cost strictly less than income m.
options.c: are preferred to every affordable bundle.
options.d: maximize utility for every possible preference ordering.

questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes the budget set from the budget line?

options.a: There is no distinction; the two terms are identical.
options.b: The budget set depends only on preferences, while the budget line depends only on technology.
options.c: The budget set contains all affordable bundles, while the budget line contains bundles that exhaust income.
options.d: The budget line contains all affordable bundles, while the budget set contains only utility-maximizing bundles.

questions.text: If good 2 is treated as a composite good representing spending on everything else, a convenient normalization is

options.d: x2 = 1 for every consumer.

questions.text: With p2 = 1, the budget constraint becomes

options.a: x1 + p1x2 ≤ m.
options.b: p1x1 + x2 ≤ m.
options.d: x1 + x2 ≤ p1m.

questions.text: For the budget line p1x1 + p2x2 = m, the vertical intercept is

options.a: m/p2.
options.b: m/p1.

questions.text: For the budget line p1x1 + p2x2 = m, the horizontal intercept is

options.a: m/p2.
options.d: m/p1.

questions.text: The slope of the budget line when x2 is on the vertical axis is

options.a: m/p2.

questions.text: The absolute value of the budget-line slope, p1/p2, measures

options.a: the opportunity cost of one unit of good 1 in units of good 2.
options.b: the consumer’s marginal utility of income.
options.c: the rate at which the consumer is willing to substitute the goods, regardless of preferences.
options.d: the amount of good 1 obtainable if all income is spent on good 2.

questions.text: Why is the budget-line slope negative when both goods have positive prices?

options.a: Relative prices must be negative for a budget constraint to bind.
options.b: Consuming more of one good while exhausting the budget requires consuming less of the other.
options.c: An increase in income always lowers consumption of both goods.
options.d: Consumers dislike both goods at the margin.

questions.text: If income increases while both prices remain unchanged, the budget line

options.a: rotates around the horizontal intercept.
options.b: shifts outward in a parallel fashion.
options.c: rotates around the vertical intercept.
options.d: becomes steeper without changing either intercept.

questions.text: If income falls while both prices remain unchanged, the budget line

options.a: does not change because relative prices are unchanged.
options.b: becomes flatter but keeps the same intercepts.
options.c: shifts inward in a parallel fashion.
options.d: rotates outward around the x1-intercept.

questions.text: If p1 rises while p2 and income remain fixed, the budget line

options.a: becomes steeper and the x1-intercept moves inward, while the x2-intercept is unchanged.
options.b: becomes flatter and the x2-intercept moves inward.
options.c: shifts outward in parallel.
options.d: keeps the same slope and both intercepts.

questions.text: If p1 falls while p2 and income remain fixed, the budget line

options.a: keeps its slope but raises the x2-intercept.
options.b: shifts inward in parallel.
options.c: becomes steeper and the x1-intercept moves inward.
options.d: becomes flatter and the x1-intercept moves outward.

questions.text: Multiplying both prices by t while holding nominal income fixed is equivalent to

options.a: adding t units of both goods to every affordable bundle.
options.b: dividing only p1 by t.
options.c: multiplying income by t while leaving prices fixed.
options.d: dividing income by t while leaving prices at their original levels.

questions.text: If p1, p2, and m are all multiplied by the same positive factor t, then

options.a: the slope changes but the intercepts do not.
options.b: the budget set expands by a factor t.
options.c: the budget set is unchanged.
options.d: the budget set shrinks by a factor t.

questions.text: Why does perfectly balanced inflation leave the budget set unchanged when income rises in the same proportion as all prices?

options.a: All real purchasing-power ratios and relative prices remain unchanged.
options.b: Every consumer purchases fixed quantities by assumption.
options.c: Nominal income is irrelevant to affordability.
options.d: Inflation necessarily changes the slope but not the intercepts.

questions.text: The numeraire is

options.a: a price normalized to 1 and used as the unit relative to which other prices and income are measured.
options.b: the good with the highest absolute price.
options.c: the consumer’s most preferred good.
options.d: the amount of income left unspent at the optimum.

questions.text: Normalizing p2 to 1 changes

options.a: the budget set unless p1 also equals 1.
options.b: the units in which prices and income are expressed, but not the underlying budget set.
options.c: the physical quantities of goods in every bundle.
options.d: the consumer’s real opportunities and preferences.

questions.text: A per-unit quantity tax t on good 1 changes its effective price from p1 to

options.a: p1/t.
options.c: p1 + t.
options.d: p1 − t.

questions.text: An ad valorem tax at rate τ on good 1 changes its effective price to

options.a: p1/τ.
options.b: p1 + τ regardless of the original price.

questions.text: A per-unit subsidy s on good 1 changes its effective price to

options.a: p1 − s.
options.c: p1 + s.
options.d: p1/s.

questions.text: An ad valorem subsidy at rate σ on good 1 changes its effective price to

options.b: σ/p1.
options.c: p1 − σ regardless of units.

questions.text: A lump-sum tax differs from a tax on good 1 because a lump-sum tax

options.a: necessarily creates a kink in the budget line.
options.b: reduces income without directly changing the relative price p1/p2.
options.c: changes only the slope of the budget line.
options.d: makes good 1 free up to a quota.

questions.text: A rationing constraint x1 ≤ x̄1

options.a: requires the consumer to buy exactly x̄1 units.
options.b: removes otherwise affordable bundles with consumption of good 1 above x̄1.
options.c: increases the horizontal intercept of the original budget line.
options.d: changes the consumer’s preferences against good 1.

questions.text: If good 1 is untaxed up to x̄1 but taxed per unit for consumption above x̄1, the budget line typically

options.a: becomes vertical at every quantity.
options.b: has a kink at x1 = x̄1.
options.c: shifts in parallel without changing slope anywhere.
options.d: remains a single straight line with the original slope.

questions.text: A policy that gives a household a fixed amount of food purchasing power rather than subsidizing every unit of food can

options.a: change preferences rather than constraints.
options.b: be represented only by a proportional increase in all prices.
options.c: never affect the shape of the budget set.
options.d: create a budget set with a kink or flat extension relative to the original cash-only budget.

questions.text: Suppose p1 = €4, p2 = €2, and m = €40. If the consumer buys one additional unit of good 1 while remaining on the budget line, how much good 2 must be forgone?

options.a: 1/2 unit of good 2.
options.b: 8 units of good 2.
options.c: 2 units of good 2.
options.d: 4 units of good 2.

questions.text: Suppose p1 = 5, p2 = 10, and m = 100. The budget line has

options.a: a slope of −1/2, an x1-intercept of 20, and an x2-intercept of 10.
options.b: a slope of 1/2, an x1-intercept of 20, and an x2-intercept of 10.
options.c: a slope of −1/2, an x1-intercept of 10, and an x2-intercept of 20.
options.d: a slope of −2, an x1-intercept of 10, and an x2-intercept of 20.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. Which change is illustrated?

options.a: An equal proportional increase in both prices and income.
options.b: A decrease in the price of good 2 with income fixed.
options.c: An increase in income with both prices fixed.
options.d: An increase in the price of good 1, holding income and the price of good 2 fixed.
